pll1d41c2-d1e3501.summary: Reports the opinion that God chose Jacob because he foresaw he would believe and serve him.

pll1d41c2-d1e3507.summary: Notes that Augustine once held this, as the Retractations show: he had argued that God did not choose works he himself would give, but chose faith in foreknowledge, choosing the one he foresaw would believe, to give him the Spirit.
claims: Augustine once held election based on foreseen faith.

pll1d41c2-d1e3529.summary: Notes that Augustine there says God chose not for works but for foreseen faith.

pll1d41c2-d1e3533.summary: Gives the retraction: he had not yet understood the election of grace (Rom 11:5), which is not grace if from merits; he would not have said 'believing is ours' had he known that faith too is God's gift. Both are ours by free will and both are given by the Spirit, since God prepares the will. So God did not choose anyone for faith or merits, nor give justifying grace for them, but chose by gratuitous goodness so that they would be good.
claims: Faith is God's gift.
Both believing and acting well are ours and God's.
God elects by gratuitous goodness, not for faith or merits.

pll1d41c2-d1e3578.summary: Cites De praedestinatione sanctorum: God did not choose because he foreknew we would be such, but so that we would be such by his election of grace.
claims: Election makes us good; it is not based on foreseen goodness.

pll1d41c2-d1e3609.summary: Raises a contrary text of Augustine on Malachi ('Jacob I loved, Esau I hated'): God's will is not unjust but comes from most hidden merits; within the one mass of sinners something precedes in some making them worthy of justification and in others of hardening.

pll1d41c2-d1e3652.summary: Notes that Augustine here seems to say the will by which God elects and reprobates comes from hidden merits, so that grace is given to some and not others for merits.

pll1d41c2-d1e3658.summary: Says it is unclear what Augustine meant, unless this is what he retracted; since other things in the same passage are explicitly retracted, it is likely this was too.
claims: Augustine probably retracted the 'hidden merits' view.

pll1d41c2-d1e3674.summary: Reports another reading: no one merits justifying grace, but some can merit having it withheld, being so wicked that they deserve rejection, while others, though not meriting grace, do not deserve to be wholly rejected. Lombard calls this frivolous.
claims: No one merits justifying grace.
The view that some merit not being rejected is frivolous.

pll1d41c2-d1e3679.summary: Notes that many, trying to explain this depth by their own conjectures, fell into fables, saying souls sinned in heaven and were sent into bodies as prisons for their merits. The Catholic faith rejects this because of Rom 9:11, 'when they were not yet born and had done nothing good or evil.' Faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge.
claims: Preexistence and prior sin of souls is rejected.
Faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge.

pll1d41c2-d1e3705.summary: Concludes that God chose by gratuitous mercy not because people would be faithful but so that they would be, and gave grace so that they would become faithful (1 Cor 7:25). Likewise he reprobated whom he willed, not for foreseen merits, but by a most right truth hidden from our senses.
claims: God chooses so that people become faithful.
Reprobation is not for foreseen merits but by hidden justice.

pll1d41c2-d1e3729.summary: Asks whether, as God elected some so that they would become good and faithful, he reprobated some so that they would be evil, and hardens them so that they sin.

pll1d41c2-d1e3732.summary: Answers that this must in no way be granted: reprobation is not the cause of evil as predestination is the cause of good, nor does hardening make a person evil as mercy makes one good.
claims: Reprobation does not cause evil.
Hardening does not make a person evil.

pl-l1d41c2.summary: Rejects the view that God chose Jacob because he foresaw his faith. Augustine once held that God chose faith in foreknowledge, but retracted it, since faith too is a merit and God's gift: both believing and acting well are ours by free will and God's by his preparing the will. So God chose not because we would be such, but so that we would be such (De praedestinatione sanctorum). Augustine's comment on Malachi that God's will comes from 'most hidden merits' seems contrary; Lombard thinks it probably among things Augustine retracted, and calls frivolous the reading that some merit not to be denied grace. Those who invented preexistent souls sinning in heaven fell into fables, contrary to Rom 9:11; faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge. God chose people not because they would be faithful but so that they would be, and reprobated by a most just, hidden truth. But one may not say God reprobated some so that they would be evil, since reprobation does not cause evil as predestination causes good.
claims: God did not choose Jacob for foreseen faith.
Augustine retracted his earlier view that God elected on foreseen faith.
Faith is also God's gift, and both believing and willing are ours and God's.
God elected so that people would be good, not because they would be.
Preexistence of souls is rejected by the Catholic faith.
Faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge.
Reprobation does not cause evil as predestination causes good.
